heroLead: Engineered, cut to length and labelled to your plan. A subfloor that arrives as a kit, goes together like one, and will not twist, shrink or feed termites for as long as the house stands.
heroPriceNote: Answer five questions and see a delivered price on screen.
overviewH2: The frame under the floor, engineered before it leaves us
overviewPara1: A steel floor frame does the job of bearers and joists, in roll-formed galvanised steel instead of timber. Posts stand on base plates, bearers sit on the posts, joists span between the bearers, and your flooring or decking goes straight over the top.
overviewPara2: Every member is rolled to its exact cut length, punched where it needs to be, and marked with the number it carries on the plan. There is no cutting list to work through on site and nothing to trim — the pieces are the lengths they are because the design says so.
overviewPara3: It suits a deck, a granny flat, a room addition, an upper floor or a mezzanine. Anywhere a subfloor has to be flat, stay flat, and be quick to stand.
advantagesH2: What it does that timber cannot
advantagesLead: None of this is a preference. These are the properties of the material, and they are the reason a steel subfloor is specified.

advantages.title: Termites have no interest in it
advantages.copy: There is nothing in a galvanised steel frame for a termite to eat. No treatment to re-apply, no inspection regime for the frame itself, and no barrier to maintain around it.

advantages.title: It does not warp, shrink or twist
advantages.copy: Steel is dimensionally stable. A floor that is flat when it is built is flat in ten years — no cupped joists, no shrinkage gaps opening in the decking, no squeaks from timber moving against a fixing.

advantages.title: It will not burn
advantages.copy: Steel is non-combustible. In a bushfire-prone area that matters to a subfloor more than almost anywhere else, because the underside of a raised floor is exactly where embers collect.

advantages.title: It will not rot
advantages.copy: Damp ground, poor drainage and a low subfloor are where timber bearers fail first. Galvanised steel is unaffected by the moisture that ends a timber frame.

advantages.title: Fewer holes to dig
advantages.copy: Steel spans further than the timber equivalent, so the frame needs fewer bearer lines — which means fewer piers, and fewer footings to excavate, set and pay for.

kitH2: A kit, not a pile of steel
kitLead: Every piece is counted, cut and labelled against the plan that comes with it. What is on the truck is what is on the drawing.

kit.name: Bearers and joists
kit.alt: Roll-formed steel bearer and joist profiles
kit.detail: The frame itself. Sized to your span, rolled to exact length, and marked with the number it carries on the plan.

kit.name: End caps
kit.alt: Pressed steel end cap that closes the end of a joist
kit.detail: Close the end of every joist and tie it to the bearer. Pre-punched at the setdown where you ask for it.

kit.name: Post to bearer connectors
kit.alt: Steel channel connector that joins a post to the bearer above it
kit.detail: Join each post to the bearer above it. Posts come in stock lengths, nested so nothing is wasted.

kit.name: Base plates
kit.alt: Steel bottom connector plate that sits between post and footing
kit.detail: Sit between the post and the footing, with the masonry anchors to fix them down.

kit.name: Fixings
kit.detail: Self-drilling tek screws throughout — counted against the frame, not estimated.

kitFootnote: Footings, subfloor bracing, balustrading and the floor surface itself are not part of the steel supply. Your quote lists what is included and what is not, item by item.
surfacesH2: What the frame is designed to carry
surfacesLead: The surface changes the framing. Tell us what is going down and the joist centres come back to suit it, rather than you finding out afterwards.

items: Compressed fibre cement 25mm, for wet areas and tile

surfacesNote: Thinner boards and a diagonal layout both need the framing closer together. We allow for it when we price your floor and tell you when we have.
faqLead: The questions that come up most often, answered the way we would answer them on the phone.

faq.a: Yes, and most people do. Every member arrives cut to length and labelled to match the plan, so the work on site is positioning and fixing rather than measuring and cutting. You will need a way to unload steel.

The frame is solved against the manufacturer's published design tables, which is not the same as site-specific certification. Footings, bracing and anything unusual about your site need an engineer. Your certifier will tell you what they want to see.

faq.q: How high can the floor be?
faq.a: Most raised floors are well within what the system handles. Past a certain height a larger post is needed and we will confirm it before quoting. Subfloor bracing and, higher again, a balustrade become a requirement — we will tell you which apply to your job.

faq.q: What if my deck is not a rectangle?
faq.a: Describe the parts, or send a sketch. L-shapes, T-shapes, steps and set-downs are all normal — the calculator handles a rectangle on screen and we work the rest through with you.

faq.q: Can I attach it to the house?
faq.a: Usually. What matters is the wall. Some substrates cannot carry the load and need a line of posts instead, which is why we ask what the wall is made of and want a photo of it.
Steel is rolled to your lengths, so it is made to order. Tell us when you need it on site and we will tell you whether that works before you commit.

faq.q: Can I have it in a colour?
faq.a: Standard supply is galvanised zinc. Powder coating is available but has to be nominated up front — it changes the price and the lead time.

faq.q: What about a beam that will not fit down the side of my house?
faq.a: Tell us the longest length that can physically reach the work area. Bearers longer than that are supplied in sections and joined over a pier, by design rather than by improvisation.
